cues.text: A Faith the World Could Not Understand
St. Agnes is remembered by the Church of Rome as among the most honored of all its virgin martyrs.
Her memory has been kept without interruption since at least the fourth century, when her feast was already recorded, together with the very road, the Via Nomentana , near which she was buried.
That a girl scarcely into her teens should be counted, from the earliest generations, among the great martyrs of the Roman Church tells us something.
The world of her time could not easily grasp it, and our own world still struggles to grasp it: holiness knows no minimum age.
A heart wholly given to Christ can show a strength beyond its years.
A Bridegroom Not of This World

Ancient tradition holds that Agnes, of a wealthy Christian family, had already consecrated her virginity to Christ when her beauty and family standing drew the attention of a young man of rank who sought her hand.
To every proposal, tradition tells us, she gave the same steady answer: that she was already pledged to a Bridegroom no earthly suitor could match.
When her suitor's advances were refused and her Christian faith revealed to the authorities, Agnes faced her trial with composure.

In an age when to be a Christian at all could still mean death, her judges found that composure first exasperating and then, we are told, unsettling — a young girl unmoved by every threat they could devise.
A Constancy Tested to the End
The accounts of Agnes's final trial were elaborated with loving detail by later Christian writers, though they rested on genuinely ancient tradition.
They tell of threats meant to break not only her body but her modesty and her spirit, and of a purity that her tormentors themselves are said to have found, in the end, untouchable.
St. Ambrose of Milan , writing several decades after her death, already knew and preached of her courage.
He told his own congregation that this girl, still very young by Roman standards, faced her executioner with a steadiness that put grown men to shame.
It was proof, he said, that the age of the body sets no limit on the strength God can pour into a consecrated soul.
Death Embraced Like a Wedding
Agnes met her death, whether by sword or by fire the earliest sources leave uncertain, with a serenity the Church has never ceased to marvel at.
Early writers describe her going to her execution as a bride goes to meet her groom, more joyful, they insist, than fearful.
This language of martyrdom as marriage to Christ would echo through the Church's language about virgin saints for centuries afterward.
A Basilica and an Unbroken Memory
During the reign of Constantine, the emperor's own daughter Constantina, healed, tradition holds, through Agnes's intercession.
She had a great basilica raised near Agnes's tomb on the Via Nomentana; the present basilica, rebuilt and modified over the centuries, still stands today, one of Rome's most treasured shrines.
To this day, on her feast of January 21, two lambs are blessed at her church in Rome.
Their wool is later woven into the pallium the pope confers on new archbishops — a small, living thread connecting the modern Church directly back to this one young Roman girl.

Her name, too, has been spoken since ancient times in the very Canon of the Mass, among the small company of holy women the whole Church holds up, Sunday after Sunday, as models of total, fearless fidelity to Christ.
Legacy
Agnes stands before every generation as a rebuke to the world's habit of measuring a person's worth by age, status, or usefulness rather than by the depth of the love a heart is capable of giving.
In a culture, ancient or modern, the human body and its purity are often treated as mere currency to be traded away.
Agnes steadfastly refused to bargain away what she had already given to Christ.
That refusal remains as luminous and necessary a witness today as it was in the Rome of the early fourth century.
